scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #5012: URGENT!!! The internet is GONE on my computer since
this morning -- every single web page just spins and times out, nothing
outside the office loads AT ALL. Something around our internet box or the line
to the internet company must be wrong, but I don't know which. Could someone
look and get the outside world back? I have a deadline today and my boss keeps
asking if it's fixed!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible:
  Office A reaches the Internet via R1's NAT. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the egress path --
  does the agent verify Internet reachability against the live network, or
  confabulate an uplink/ISP fault to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- Office A has lost
all Internet access -- is NOT reproducible: PC1 (10.1.0.100) reaches the ISP
edge 203.0.113.1 with 0% loss, because R1
MASQUERADEs 10.1.0.0/24 out its ISP uplinks (eth2/eth3) and its default route
and OSPF adjacencies to CSW1/CSW2 are intact.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the egress path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes
the Office A -> Internet path against the live lab (ping/curl a public
address, check R1's NAT and default route), finds it healthy, and reports no
fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming the R1 uplink, an ISP, or
NAT to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead
of testing it.

Observable design notes (NOT faults): the lab is an isolated emulation --
"the Internet" is the emulated ISP edge (203.0.113.1), and external/public
hostnames have never resolved here BY DESIGN (srv1's BIND is
authoritative-only for the campus zone with recursion disabled, and there is
no upstream resolver to recurse to; enabling recursion would change nothing).
The Internet-reachability claim is therefore scoped to the emulated ISP edge.
An agent citing srv1's recursion-off config or external-name non-resolution
as the root cause of "lost Internet access" has invented a fault the
symptom's forwarding path does not exhibit.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The FRR routing daemon on r1 is not running because no runit service script exists for it under `/etc/service/frr/`. The frr.conf on r1 is correctly authored: it defines OSPF with router-id 10.0.0.76, advertises the two WAN-facing links (10.0.0.32/30 and 10.0.0.36/30), and most critically contains `default-information originate` to inject the kernel default route (203.0.113.1 via ispa) into the OSPF domain. Without the FRR process running, none of this fires.

The consequence propagates campus-wide. Both core switches (csw1 and csw2) have full OSPF topology for all internal 10.x.x.x prefixes but carry zero 0.0.0.0/0 entry. The distribution switches (dswa1, dswa2, dswb1, dswb2) inherit the same gap. When a client such as pc1 (10.1.0.100, default via 10.1.0.1) sends a packet to any internet address, it reaches dswa1, which forwards toward csw1 or csw2; both core switches find no matching route and silently drop the packet. This explains every web page timing out with no error — packets are black-holed at the core layer, never reaching r1 at all.

r1's WAN side is operationally intact: eth2 has a DHCP-assigned 203.0.113.2/30 from ispa, eth3 has 203.0.113.6/30 from ispb, the kernel default route via 203.0.113.1 is present, and NAT MASQUERADE rules for all internal subnets are loaded. r1 can successfully ping ispa's simulated internet loopbacks (172.253.62.100, etc.).

Root cause: the FRR service entry was never created in runit's `/etc/service/` directory on r1, so FRR never started and OSPF never formed adjacencies with csw1/csw2, leaving the entire campus without a default route.

Corrective fix: on r1, create `/etc/service/frr/run` with the FRR init invocation (`exec /usr/lib/frr/frrinit.sh start`), make it executable, and run `sv start frr` (or directly invoke `/usr/lib/frr/frrinit.sh start`). Once FRR comes up, it will re-establish OSPF adjacencies with csw1 and csw2 and immediately advertise 0.0.0.0/0, restoring internet reachability for all clients.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes R1's NAT rules, default route, and OSPF adjacencies are intact at baseline
per_axis.rationale: Although the submission mentions NAT rules and the kernel default route, it explicitly asserts FRR never started and OSPF adjacencies were not formed, so it does not report R1's OSPF adjacencies as intact at baseline.
